newsitem.title: UK: UK firms told to ease up on rules,focus on profits.
newsitem.headline: UK firms told to ease up on rules,focus on profits.

text.p: British companies were on Tuesday told they should think more about their bottom line and less about the fine print in the rulebook.

The long-awaited Hampel committee report on corporate governance -- the way a firm conducts itself -- said companies and shareholders should be more flexible and less driven by "box-ticking", where rules are interpreted too literally. Ronald Hampel, chairman of ICI and head of the committee, said governance was about both prosperity and accountability but in recent years the balance had swung in favour of being accountable.
"We are anxious to see that balance corrected," Hampel told a news briefing but added this did not diminish the importance of accountability.
"It is vital to recognise that what boards are about in all listed companies is about increasing the prosperity of the particular company over time."
Hampel said his preliminary report, which has taken 18 months of consultation and discussion to prepare, that the box ticking approach was neither fair to firms or efficient in preventing abuse.

He said the process of establishing principles and rules for corporate governance was more about "evolution than revolution". His report follows the earlier Cadbury code on governance and the Greenbury report on executive pay which are a part of the London Stock Exchange's listing requirements.
The Hampel report said its principles should be become an additional regulatory requirement but could "conveniently be linked" with the listing requirements.
It says firms and shareholders should apply broad principles "flexibly, with common sense and with due regard to companies' individual circumstances".

Hampel said the principles should apply to all firms equally and should not distinguish between small and large companies. But the interpretation of these principles should be flexible, so smaller firms were not burdened with costs they could not afford.

The report was welcomed by the director general of the Institute of Directors (IoD) Tim Melville-Ross who said it enshrined the idea companies should observe the spirit rather than the letter of such principles.
Melville-Ross told Reuters that companies should be allowed "sufficient flexibility to move fast in a competitive environment".
"The last thing you want is for shareholders to start coming in and running the company," he added.
While the Institute of Chartered Accountants also welcomed the interim report, due to be completed by the end of the year after a comment period, Britain's Trades Union Congress (TUC) slammed it.

"The weakness of the report shows that the voluntary approach has reached its limit. We are now looking to the government to tackle corporate excess and short-termism in industry," TUC deputy general secretary Brendan Barber said in a statement.
The TUC also raised concerns about the treatment of so-called stakeholders, including employees and customers and the wider community.
But this approach of direct accountability to stakeholders was not supported by the report.
"We are clear that boards are responsible to shareholders and to divide that responsibility would be to make them and their supervision less effective," Hampel said.
He said the idea of individual stakeholder representation on a board was not a factor in corporate success.
Hampel said the report had paid great attention to the balance of a company's board of directors, the need for independent non-executive directors and a lead non-executive director to be identified.
When first appointed, directors should be given appropriate instruction and this should be renewed as necessary in subsequent years.

It also found there was overwhelming support in Britain to stick with the system of "a properly balanced unitary board" and virtually none for a two-tier board involving supervisory directors. Other recommendations of the report included companies providing a narrative account of how they apply the broad principles in their annual report.
It suggested a flexible approach to the Cadbury recommendation that the roles of chairman and chief executive, although it said separation was to be preferred and combination should be justified.
On the controversial issue of remuneration, which has roused public indignation towards so-called "fat cat" directors, Hampel's report does not suggest further refinement of the Greenbury code.

Hampel said total rewards from performance schemes "should not be excessive", but the report saw no objection to paying non-executives in company shares, while not recommending it as a universal practice.

While stopping short of recommending voting by institutional shareholders should be forced to vote at meetings, the report said they had an obligation to their clients to "adopt a considered policy on voting their shares'.

And pension fund trustees should encourage fund managers "to take a long view in managing their investments", the report added. Hampel also suggested shareholder bodies the Association of British Insurers and National Association of Pension Funds should examine a problem caused by the existence of different and incompatible shareholder voting guidelines.
